questions.sub_topic: Hypotonic vs Hypertonic Solutions
questions.question: When red blood cells (RBCs) are placed in a hypertonic aqueous sodium chloride solution (concentration > 0.9% w/v):
options: A) Water flows out of the cells by osmosis, causing them to shrink (plasmolysis)
B) Water flows into the cells causing them to swell and burst (hemolysis)
C) The cells remain completely unchanged in size and shape
D) Sodium chloride crystals precipitate inside the nucleus
questions.explanation: In hypertonic solution (osmotic pressure higher than 0.9% saline), water leaves the erythrocyte by exosmosis down its chemical potential gradient, causing shrinkage.

questions.sub_topic: Vapour Pressure of Multi-Component Liquid Mixture
questions.question: An ideal solution is prepared by mixing 2 moles of liquid A (\( P_A^\circ = 400 \text{ mm Hg} \)) and 3 moles of liquid B (\( P_B^\circ = 200 \text{ mm Hg} \)). The total vapour pressure of the solution at equilibrium is:

questions.sub_topic: Mole Fraction in Vapour Phase Dalton-Raoult
questions.question: For the ideal solution in the previous question (\( P_A = 160 \text{ mm Hg} \), \( P_{\text{total}} = 280 \text{ mm Hg} \)), the mole fraction of component A in the vapour phase (\( y_A \)) is:
questions.explanation: According to Dalton's law of partial pressures: \( y_A = P_A / P_{\text{total}} = 160 / 280 = 4/7 \approx 0.571 \).

questions.sub_topic: Elevation in Boiling Point Thermodynamic Derivation
questions.question: The molal boiling point elevation constant (ebullioscopic constant, \( K_b \)) is related to the thermodynamic properties of the solvent by:
options: B) \( K_b = \frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{1000 R T_b M} \)
questions.explanation: Thermodynamic derivation from the Clausius-Clapeyron equation gives \( K_b = \frac{R T_b^2 M_1}{1000 \Delta_{\text{vap}} H} = \frac{R T_b^2}{1000 l_v} \), where \( M_1 \) is solvent molar mass and \( l_v \) is latent heat of vaporization.

questions.sub_topic: Freezing Point of Complex Coordination Salt
questions.question: A 0.01 m aqueous solution of \( [\ce{Co(NH3)5Cl}]\ce{Cl2} \) is prepared. Assuming complete (100%) dissociation into ions, what is the expected freezing point of the solution? (\( K_f \) of water = 1.86 K kg/mol)
questions.explanation: \( [\ce{Co(NH3)5Cl}]\ce{Cl2} -> [\ce{Co(NH3)5Cl}]^{2+} + 2\ce{Cl^-} \) gives \( n = 3 \) particles per formula unit, so \( i = 3 \). \( \Delta T_f = i K_f m = 3 \times 1.86 \times 0.01 = 0.0558 \text{ K} \). Freezing point = \( -0.0558^\circ\text{C} \).

questions.sub_topic: Kohlrausch Law: Limiting Conductivity of Polyprotic Salt
questions.question: According to Kohlrausch's law, the limiting molar conductivity of aluminium sulfate, \( \ce{Al2(SO4)3} \), is given by:
questions.explanation: Dissociation: \( \ce{Al2(SO4)3 -> 2Al^{3+} + 3SO4^{2-}} \). Thus \( \Lambda_m^\circ = 2\lambda^\circ(\ce{Al^{3+}}) + 3\lambda^\circ(\ce{SO4^{2-}}) \).

questions.sub_topic: Faraday Current Efficiency Calculation
questions.question: A steady electric current of 2.0 A is passed for 965 seconds through a copper plating bath. If 0.508 g of copper is deposited (atomic mass of Cu = 63.5 u), what is the current efficiency?
questions.explanation: Charge \( Q = 2.0 \times 965 = 1930 \text{ C} \). Theoretical mass \( w_{\text{theo}} = \frac{E \cdot Q}{F} = \frac{(63.5/2) \times 1930}{96500} = \frac{31.75 \times 1930}{96500} = 0.635 \text{ g} \). Efficiency = \( \frac{0.508}{0.635} \times 100 = 80\% \).

questions.sub_topic: Thermodynamics of Lead-Acid Cell Discharge
questions.question: In the lead storage battery, the standard EMF is \( E^\circ = 2.04 \text{ V} \) at 298 K for \( n=2 \). The standard Gibbs free energy change (\( \Delta G^\circ \)) of the discharge reaction is:
questions.explanation: \( \Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 2.04 = -393,720 \text{ J/mol} \approx -393.7 \text{ kJ/mol} \).

questions.sub_topic: Nernst Equation for Polyvalent Redox Couple
questions.question: For the redox half-cell \( \ce{Cr2O7^{2-}(aq) + 14H+(aq) + 6e^- -> 2Cr^{3+}(aq) + 7H2O(l)} \) at 298 K, if the pH is increased by 1 unit while keeping all other concentrations at 1 M, the reduction potential:
questions.explanation: \( E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{6} \log \frac{[\ce{Cr^{3+}}]^2}{[\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}][\ce{H+}]^{14}} = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591 \times 14}{6} \text{pH} = E^\circ - 0.1379 \times \text{pH} \). Increasing pH by 1 decreases \( E \) by 0.138 V.

questions.sub_topic: Potentiometric Titration Equivalence Point Potential
questions.question: In the potentiometric redox titration of \( \ce{Fe^{2+}} \) (\( E^\circ = 0.77 \text{ V} \)) with \( \ce{Ce^{4+}} \) (\( E^\circ = 1.44 \text{ V} \)), the theoretical potential at the equivalence point at 298 K is:
questions.explanation: At equivalence point, \( [\ce{Fe^{3+}}] = [\ce{Ce^{3+}}] \) and \( [\ce{Fe^{2+}}] = [\ce{Ce^{4+}}] \). Adding Nernst expressions gives \( 2E = E^\circ_{\ce{Fe}} + E^\circ_{\ce{Ce}} \Rightarrow E = \frac{0.77 + 1.44}{2} = 1.105 \text{ V} \).

questions.sub_topic: Units of Rate Constant for Order n/2
questions.question: For a fractional reaction of order \( n = 3/2 \), the SI units of the rate constant \( k \) are:

questions.sub_topic: Fraction of Molecules Possessing Activation Energy Calculation
questions.question: At 300 K, a reaction has an activation energy \( E_a = 57.4 \text{ kJ/mol} \). What is the value of the Boltzmann fraction \( e^{-E_a / (RT)} \)? (\( R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} \), \( \ln 10 = 2.303 \))

questions.sub_topic: Enzyme Kinetics: Lineweaver-Burk Double Reciprocal Plot
questions.question: In enzyme-catalyzed reactions obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics, a linear Lineweaver-Burk plot of \( 1/v \) versus \( 1/[S] \) has:
options: A) Slope = \( V_{\text{max}} / K_m \) and y-intercept = \( K_m \)
B) Slope = \( K_m / V_{\text{max}} \) and y-intercept = \( 1 / V_{\text{max}} \)
questions.explanation: Taking reciprocal of \( v = \frac{V_{\text{max}}[S]}{K_m + [S]} \) gives \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{K_m}{V_{\text{max}}} \left(\frac{1}{[S]}\right) + \frac{1}{V_{\text{max}}} \), a line with slope \( K_m/V_{\text{max}} \) and y-intercept \( 1/V_{\text{max}} \) (x-intercept = \( -1/K_m \)).

questions.sub_topic: Kinetics of Branching Chain Reactions (Explosion Limits)
questions.question: In branching chain reactions (such as the combustion of hydrogen \( \ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O} \)), the sudden transition from slow reaction to violent explosion at the lower explosion limit occurs because:
options: A) The rate of chain branching exceeds the rate of chain termination by wall deactivation
B) All reactant molecules undergo spontaneous nuclear fusion
C) The activation energy drops instantly to zero
D) The container experiences sudden vacuum collapse
questions.explanation: At low pressures, chain carriers hit the walls and terminate. Once pressure rises to the first explosion limit, gas-phase chain-branching steps outpace wall destruction, leading to exponential multiplication of radicals and explosion.

questions.sub_topic: Primary Kinetic Salt Effect Bronsted-Bjerrum
questions.question: According to the Brønsted-Bjerrum equation for reactions between ions \( A^{z_A} \) and \( B^{z_B} \), increasing the ionic strength of the solution causes the rate constant to:
options: A) Always increase regardless of ionic charge signs
B) Increase if \( z_A \) and \( z_B \) have the same sign (like charges), but decrease if they have opposite signs
C) Always decrease regardless of ionic charge signs
D) Remain completely independent of ionic strength
questions.explanation: \( \log k = \log k_0 + 2 A z_A z_B \sqrt{I} \). When \( z_A z_B > 0 \) (like charges), rate increases with \( \sqrt{I} \); when \( z_A z_B < 0 \) (opposite charges), rate decreases with \( \sqrt{I} \).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Electronic Configuration of Curium and Berkelium
questions.question: Curium (\( Z = 96 \)) exhibits a half-filled 5f subshell analogous to gadolinium in lanthanoids. Its ground-state valence configuration is:
questions.explanation: Curium has configuration \( [\ce{Rn}] 5f^7 6d^1 7s^2 \) to preserve the extra thermodynamic exchange stability of a half-filled \( 5f^7 \) shell.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Disproportionation of Manganate in Acidic Solution
questions.question: In acidic solution, green manganate(VI) ions (\( \ce{MnO4^{2-}} \)) are unstable and disproportionate spontaneously into:
options: A) Purple permanganate (\( \ce{MnO4^-} \)) and brown manganese dioxide (\( \ce{MnO2} \))
B) Colourless \( \ce{Mn^{2+}} \) and oxygen gas only
C) Manganese metal and ozone gas
questions.explanation: \( \ce{3MnO4^{2-} + 4H+ -> 2MnO4^- + MnO2 + 2H2O} \). Manganese(+6) simultaneously oxidizes to +7 (permanganate) and reduces to +4 (manganese dioxide).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: High Melting Points of W, Mo, Cr
questions.question: Tungsten (W) has the highest melting point (3422°C) among all metals because:
options: A) Tungsten has the lowest density of all elements
B) Tungsten atoms are held by hydrogen bonds
C) Tungsten forms ionic crystals with atmospheric oxygen
D) Maximum number of unpaired 5d electrons form exceptionally strong covalent metallic bonds in the crystal lattice
questions.explanation: In group 6 (Cr, Mo, W), valence configuration is \( (n-1)d^5 ns^1 \) with 6 unpaired electrons. In tungsten, large 5d orbital overlap gives maximal interatomic metallic bonding strength.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Lanthanoid Contraction vs Actinoid Contraction Comparison
questions.question: Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction because:
options: A) 5f electrons have poorer shielding capability than 4f electrons due to their more diffuse spatial distribution
B) 5f orbitals have smaller principal quantum number than 4f
C) Actinoids have lower effective nuclear charge than lanthanoids
D) Actinoid nuclei emit continuous alpha particles
questions.explanation: The 5f orbitals are more diffuse and extend further from the nucleus than 4f orbitals; consequently, 5f electrons shield each other less effectively against increasing nuclear charge.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Permanganate Oxidation of Oxalate in Acidic Solution
questions.question: In the titration of acidified \( \ce{KMnO4} \) against warm oxalic acid, the reaction is initially slow but accelerates rapidly as it proceeds because of:
options: A) Continuous evaporation of water molecules
B) Decomposition of oxalic acid into methane gas
C) Autocatalysis by the product manganese(II) ions (\( \ce{Mn^{2+}} \))
questions.explanation: The reaction \( \ce{2MnO4^- + 5C2O4^{2-} + 16H+ -> 2Mn^{2+} + 10CO2 + 8H2O} \) is autocatalytic; the generated \( \ce{Mn^{2+}} \) acts as a catalyst that accelerates subsequent oxidation steps.

questions.sub_topic: Polydentate Chelation Thermodynamics
questions.question: The enhanced thermodynamic stability of chelate complexes over analogous complexes with unidentate ligands is primarily driven by:
options: A) A large positive entropy change (\( \Delta S > 0 \)) resulting from the release of coordinated water molecules
B) A huge decrease in temperature during complexation
C) The total destruction of ligand molecules
D) Complete cancellation of nuclear charges
questions.explanation: When a multidentate ligand displaces چندین monodentate water molecules, the total number of free independent particles in solution increases, giving \( \Delta S > 0 \) and favorable \( \Delta G < 0 \).

questions.sub_topic: Magnetic Properties of Tetrachloromanganate(II)
questions.question: The complex ion \( [\ce{MnCl4}]^{2-} \) is tetrahedral and has a \( 3d^5 \) configuration. Its spin-only magnetic moment is:
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral fields are always weak-field, so all 5 d-electrons remain unpaired: \( e^2 t_2^3 \) (\( n=5 \)). \( \mu = \sqrt{5(7)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92 \text{ BM} \).

questions.sub_topic: Spectrochemical Series: Halide vs Carbonyl Field Strength
questions.question: Why is iodide (\( \ce{I^-} \)) at the lowest end of the spectrochemical series (weakest field) while carbon monoxide (\( \ce{CO} \)) is at the highest end (strongest field)?
options: A) \( \ce{I^-} \) has a smaller ionic radius than \( \ce{CO} \)
B) Carbon monoxide donates protons to the metal center
C) Iodide cannot form coordinate covalent sigma bonds
D) \( \ce{I^-} \) is a strong pi-donor ligand that destabilizes \( t_{2g} \) orbitals, whereas \( \ce{CO} \) is a strong pi-acceptor ligand that stabilizes \( t_{2g} \) orbitals
questions.explanation: \( \pi \)-donor ligands (like halides) donate electrons from filled p-orbitals to metal \( t_{2g} \), raising \( t_{2g} \) energy and decreasing \( \Delta_o \). \( \pi \)-acceptor ligands (like \( \ce{CO} \)) accept back-bonding into \( \pi^* \), lowering \( t_{2g} \) and maximizing \( \Delta_o \).

questions.sub_topic: Trans Effect in Square Planar Platinum Substitution
questions.question: The trans effect in square planar platinum(II) complexes directs substitution of the ligand situated trans to which group in the order:
options: C) \( \ce{CN^- \approx CO \approx C2H4 > PR3 > NO2^- > I^- > Br^- > Cl^- > NH3 > H2O} \)
D) All ligands exhibit identical trans-directing abilities
questions.explanation: The trans effect is the labilization of ligands trans to a specific directing group; strong \( \pi \)-acceptors (\( \ce{CN^-, CO, C2H4} \)) and polarizable ligands exhibit the strongest trans effect.

questions.sub_topic: Orgel Diagram Transitions for d1 and d9 Octahedral Complexes
questions.question: In an octahedral crystal field, the absorption spectrum of \( d^1 \) (\( \ce{Ti^{3+}} \)) consists of a single electronic transition, corresponding to:
questions.explanation: The Russell-Saunders ground term for \( d^1 \) is \( {}^2D \), which splits in an octahedral field into a lower \( {}^2T_{2g} \) term and upper \( {}^2E_g \) term; absorption promotes an electron between these states.

questions.sub_topic: Allylic Bromination with NBS
questions.question: Treatment of propene (\( \ce{CH3-CH=CH2} \)) with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) in \( \ce{CCl4} \) under light yields:
questions.explanation: NBS provides a low steady-state concentration of \( \ce{Br2} \) in non-polar solvent, favoring free-radical allylic hydrogen abstraction to form resonance-stabilized allyl radicals that yield allyl bromide.

questions.sub_topic: Nucleophilic Substitution of Neopentyl Halides
questions.question: Neopentyl bromide (\( (\ce{CH3})_3\ce{C-CH2Br} \)) is a primary alkyl halide that undergoes \( \text{S}_\text{N}2 \) substitution exceptionally slowly because:
options: A) The C-Br bond has 100% ionic character
B) Neopentyl bromide cannot dissolve in organic solvents
C) The molecule is completely planar
D) Extreme steric crowding from the bulky tert-butyl group blocks backside attack by nucleophiles
questions.explanation: Although the reacting carbon is primary, the three methyl groups on the \( \beta \)-carbon (tert-butyl) create massive steric hindrance against backside nucleophilic attack, reducing \( \text{S}_\text{N}2 \) rates by a factor of \( 10^5 \).

questions.sub_topic: Mechanism of Chloroform Hydrolysis to Formate
questions.question: Hydrolysis of chloroform (\( \ce{CHCl3} \)) with hot aqueous potassium hydroxide yields:
questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution of three chlorines gives the unstable ortho-formic acid \( \ce{CH(OH)3} \), which immediately loses water to form formic acid, neutralized by KOH to potassium formate.

questions.sub_topic: Biphenyl Chirality: Atropisomerism in Substituted Biphenyls
questions.question: 2,2'-Dinitro-6,6'-dicarboxybiphenyl is optically active and can be resolved into stable enantiomers despite lacking any asymmetric carbon atoms because of:
options: A) Rapid inversion of tetrahedral carbon atoms
B) Delocalization of electrons into a non-planar vacuum
C) Restricted rotation about the central C-C single bond caused by steric hindrance of bulky ortho substituents (atropisomerism)
questions.explanation: Bulky ortho substituents prevent the two aromatic rings from becoming coplanar; restricted rotation around the pivot bond creates perpendicular non-superimposable chiral conformers (atropisomers).

questions.sub_topic: Kinetics of SN1 vs SN2: Solvent Polarity Effect
questions.question: Increasing the polarity and ionizing power of the solvent (e.g. changing from ethanol to water) causes the rate of an \( \text{S}_\text{N}1 \) reaction to:
options: C) Convert the reaction into free-radical chlorination
D) Increase markedly, because polar solvent molecules solvate and stabilize the charge-separated transition state and carbocation intermediate
questions.explanation: In \( \text{S}_\text{N}1 \), neutral substrate dissociates into a charged carbocation and halide anion; polar protic solvents stabilize this polar transition state through dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding, lowering \( \Delta G^\ddagger \).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Industrial Preparation of Methanol
questions.question: Methanol is commercially manufactured on a large scale by catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide using:
options: A) Nickel catalyst at room temperature and 1 atm
B) Concentrated sulfuric acid in boiling water
C) A catalyst mixture of \( \ce{ZnO-Cr2O3} \) at 573–673 K and 200–300 atm pressure
D) Platinum gauze at 1000 K without pressure
questions.explanation: \( \ce{CO + 2H2 ->[ZnO-Cr2O3, 573-673 K, 200-300 atm] CH3OH} \). This is the modern industrial synthesis of methanol from synthesis gas.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Cumene Hydroperoxide Cleavage Mechanism Details
questions.question: In the industrial synthesis of phenol from cumene hydroperoxide (\( \ce{C6H5-C(CH3)2-O-OH} \)), acid treatment triggers a rearrangement where which group migrates to oxygen?
options: A) A methyl group migrates to the oxygen atom
B) The hydroperoxide group detaches as hydrogen peroxide
C) The cumene ring undergoes complete ring expansion to a seven-membered ring
D) The phenyl group migrates to the electron-deficient oxygen atom with loss of water
questions.explanation: Protonation of the terminal -OH followed by departure of \( \ce{H2O} \) creates an electron-deficient oxygen; the phenyl group has higher migratory aptitude than methyl and migrates to oxygen, forming a carbocation that hydrolyzes to phenol and acetone.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Mechanism of Reimer-Tiemann Dichlorocarbene Intermediate
questions.question: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction of phenol with chloroform and \( \ce{NaOH} \), the initial reactive species generated by \( \alpha \)-elimination of chloroform is:
options: A) Trichloromethyl carbanion (\( \ce{^-CCl3} \)) acting as a nucleophile
B) Dichlorocarbene (\( \ce{:CCl2} \)), an electrophilic singlet carbene
questions.explanation: Hydroxide abstracts the acidic proton of chloroform: \( \ce{CHCl3 + OH^- <=> H2O + ^-CCl3 -> :CCl2 + Cl^-} \). Dichlorocarbene is an electron-deficient electrophile that attacks the phenoxide ring.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Selective Oxidation of Diols with Periodic Acid (Malaprade Reaction)
questions.question: Oxidative cleavage of a vicinal diol (e.g. butane-2,3-diol) with periodic acid (\( \ce{HIO4} \)) yields:
options: A) Two molecules of acetic acid
questions.explanation: Periodic acid selectively cleaves the C-C bond of vicinal diols via a cyclic periodate ester intermediate, converting each \( \ce{-CH(OH)-} \) unit into an aldehyde: \( \ce{CH3CH(OH)CH(OH)CH3 ->[HIO4] 2CH3CHO + HIO3 + H2O} \).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Crown Ether Cation Complexation Specificity
questions.question: 18-Crown-6 binds potassium ions (\( \ce{K+} \)) with exceptional selectivity over sodium (\( \ce{Na+} \)) and lithium (\( \ce{Li+} \)) ions because:
options: A) Potassium ions have negative electric charge
B) Sodium ions are completely insoluble in organic solvents
C) Crown ethers form covalent C-K bonds
D) The ionic diameter of \( \ce{K+} \) (2.66 Å) matches the internal cavity diameter of 18-crown-6 (2.6–3.2 Å) almost perfectly
questions.explanation: Crown ethers possess interior polar cavities lined with ether oxygens. The cavity size of 18-crown-6 precisely complements the ionic radius of \( \ce{K+} \), giving maximum non-covalent binding affinity.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Stephen Reaction Intermediate Hydrolysis
questions.question: In the Stephen reduction, ethanenitrile treated with \( \ce{SnCl2 + HCl} \) forms an intermediate aldimine hydrochloride which upon boiling with water yields:
questions.explanation: \( \ce{CH3-CN ->[SnCl2/HCl] CH3-CH=NH.HCl ->[H2O, \Delta] CH3-CHO + NH4Cl} \). The aldimine salt hydrolyzes cleanly to acetaldehyde.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Reformatsky Reaction with Alpha-Halo Esters
questions.question: The Reformatsky reaction involves the condensation of an aldehyde or ketone with an \( \alpha \)-halo ester in the presence of zinc metal to synthesize:
questions.explanation: Zinc inserts into the \( \ce{C-Br} \) bond of an \( \alpha \)-bromoester to form an organozinc enolate (Reformatsky reagent), which nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl group to give a \( \beta \)-hydroxy ester.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Favorskii Rearrangement of Alpha-Halo Ketones
questions.question: Treatment of an \( \alpha \)-haloketone with hydroxide or alkoxide base results in skeletal rearrangement to a carboxylic acid or ester via a cyclopropanone intermediate. This is known as the:
questions.explanation: The Favorskii rearrangement involves base abstraction of an \( \alpha' \)-proton, intramolecular nucleophilic displacement forming a cyclopropanone, and subsequent ring opening to yield an ester or carboxylic acid.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Mechanism of Benzilic Acid Rearrangement
questions.question: When benzil (\( \ce{C6H5-CO-CO-C6H5} \)) is treated with aqueous potassium hydroxide, it rearranges to potassium benzilate (\( \ce{(C6H5)2C(OH)COOK} \)). Mechanistically, this reaction involves:
options: A) Direct oxidative cleavage into two moles of benzoic acid
B) Homolytic radical cleavage of the central C-C single bond
D) Reversible addition of hydroxide ion to one carbonyl group followed by a 1,2-phenyl shift to the adjacent carbonyl carbon
questions.explanation: Hydroxide attacks one carbonyl carbon, and the resulting oxyanion promotes a 1,2-phenyl shift with its electron pair to the adjacent carbonyl group, followed by rapid proton transfer to form benzilate.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Ortho Effect in Substituted Benzoic Acids
questions.question: Ortho-substituted benzoic acids (e.g. o-toluic acid, o-chlorobenzoic acid) are stronger acids than benzoic acid and their meta/para isomers, regardless of whether the ortho substituent is electron-donating or electron-withdrawing, because of:
options: A) Direct covalent bonding between the ortho substituent and acidic hydrogen
B) The ortho effect (steric hindrance forces the carboxyl group out of the aromatic plane, inhibiting resonance with the ring and facilitating carboxylate ionization)
C) Complete destruction of aromaticity in the benzene ring
D) Formation of coordinate bonds with solvent water
questions.explanation: Steric hindrance from ortho substituents forces the \( \ce{-COOH} \) group out of coplanarity with the benzene ring. This minimizes resonance electron donation from the ring into the carbonyl carbon, increasing acid strength (ortho effect).

questions.sub_topic: Basicity Constant Kb and pKb Relationship
questions.question: For a series of amines in aqueous solution, a smaller value of \( \text{p}K_b \) corresponds to:
options: B) A stronger basic strength (larger \( K_b \))
C) Higher acidity than hydrochloric acid
D) Zero tendency to accept protons
questions.explanation: \( \text{p}K_b = -\log K_b \). A larger \( K_b \) value reflects a greater extent of ionization in water, which mathematically corresponds to a smaller \( \text{p}K_b \).

questions.sub_topic: Sandmeyer Reaction Cyanation Mechanism
questions.question: In the conversion of benzenediazonium chloride to benzonitrile using \( \ce{CuCN} \), the cuprous ion acts as a:
options: A) Permanent structural component of the nitrile product
B) Strong dehydrating agent removing water
C) Catalyst that facilitates one-electron redox transfer to generate aryl radicals
D) Lewis acid converting benzene into cyclohexane
questions.explanation: Sandmeyer reactions proceed via single-electron transfer (SET): \( \ce{Cu(I)} \) reduces \( \ce{ArN2+} \) to an aryl radical \( \ce{Ar^.} \) and \( \ce{N2} \), which then combines with \( \ce{Cu(II)(CN)2} \) to yield \( \ce{ArCN} \) and regenerate \( \ce{Cu(I)} \).

questions.sub_topic: Mechanism of Carbylamine Reaction: Dichlorocarbene Intermediate
questions.question: In the carbylamine test for primary amines with \( \ce{CHCl3} \) and \( \ce{KOH} \), the reactive electrophilic intermediate that attacks the amine nitrogen is:
questions.explanation: Base deprotonates chloroform to give \( \ce{^-CCl3} \), which eliminates \( \ce{Cl^-} \) to yield electrophilic \( \ce{:CCl2} \). Nucleophilic attack by \( \ce{RNH2} \) followed by two dehydrochlorinations yields the isocyanide \( \ce{R-N#C} \).

questions.sub_topic: Hofmann Elimination of Quaternary Ammonium Hydroxides
questions.question: Thermal decomposition of a quaternary ammonium hydroxide (Hofmann elimination) yields predominantly the least substituted alkene (Hofmann product) rather than the Saytzeff product because:
options: A) Tertiary amines undergo spontaneous nuclear fission
B) The least substituted alkene has higher thermodynamic stability
C) Steric bulk of the trialkylamino leaving group and high acidity of less sterically hindered beta-hydrogens govern the transition state
D) Hydroxide ion dissolves the double bond
questions.explanation: The bulky \( \ce{-N(CH3)3+} \) group causes extreme steric crowding, and its strong -I effect makes the least substituted \( \beta \)-hydrogens most acidic. Base abstracts the least hindered proton, yielding the less substituted alkene.

questions.sub_topic: Sommelet-Hauser Rearrangement of Benzylic Quaternary Salts
questions.question: When benzylic quaternary ammonium salts are treated with strong base (such as sodium amide), they undergo a [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement to yield ortho-substituted tertiary amines. This reaction is known as the:
questions.explanation: Deprotonation of benzylic quaternary ammonium salts forms an ylide that undergoes an aromatic [2,3]-sigmatropic shift followed by rearomatization to form ortho-substituted benzylamines (Sommelet-Hauser rearrangement).

questions.sub_topic: Composition of Invert Sugar
questions.question: Hydrolysis of sucrose yields an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose known as invert sugar, whose net optical rotation is:
questions.explanation: Sucrose is dextrorotatory (+66.5°). On hydrolysis: D-(+)-glucose (+52.7°) and D-(-)-fructose (-92.4°) give a net optical rotation of \( \frac{+52.7 - 92.4}{2} = -19.85^\circ \) (net laevorotatory).

questions.sub_topic: Conformational Analysis of Beta-D-Glucopyranose
questions.question: \( \beta \)-D-Glucopyranose is the most thermodynamically stable aldohexose in aqueous solution because in its chair conformation (4C1):
options: A) All five non-hydrogen substituents (four -OH groups and the -CH2OH group) occupy equatorial positions
B) All substituents occupy axial positions
C) The molecule is completely planar without 1,3-diaxial interactions
D) It forms a permanent covalent triple bond with water
questions.explanation: In the \( {}^4C_1 \) chair form of \( \beta \)-D-glucopyranose, every hydroxyl group and the bulky \( \ce{-CH2OH} \) group are equatorial, minimizing 1,3-diaxial steric and dipole repulsions.

questions.sub_topic: Ramachandran Plot Allowed Phi-Psi Angles
questions.question: In structural biochemistry, a Ramachandran plot maps the sterically allowed conformational angles of a polypeptide backbone by plotting:
options: A) The bond lengths of peptide bonds versus molecular mass
B) The optical rotation versus temperature
C) The number of hydrogen bonds versus pH
D) The dihedral torsion angles phi (\( \phi \)) versus psi (\( \psi \)) around the alpha-carbon
questions.explanation: The Ramachandran plot maps the backbone torsion angles \( \phi \) (\( \ce{N-C_\alpha} \)) and \( \psi \) (\( \ce{C_\alpha-C} \)) to identify sterically allowed conformations such as \( \alpha \)-helices and \( \beta \)-sheets.

questions.sub_topic: Chemical Cleavage of Peptides with Cyanogen Bromide
questions.question: In protein sequencing, cyanogen bromide (CNBr) selectively cleaves polypeptide chains at the carboxyl side of which specific amino acid residue?
questions.explanation: Cyanogen bromide specifically reacts with the nucleophilic thioether sulfur of methionine residues, forming a peptidyl homoserine lactone and cleaving the peptide bond specifically at the C-terminus of methionine.

questions.sub_topic: Sanger Dideoxy DNA Sequencing Chain Termination
questions.question: In the Sanger dideoxy method of DNA sequencing, 2',3'-dideoxynucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) terminate polynucleotide chain elongation because:
options: A) They lack a nitrogenous base
B) They destroy the DNA polymerase enzyme irreversibly
C) They lack a 3'-hydroxyl group (-OH) required for the formation of the next phosphodiester bond
D) They convert the DNA template into single-stranded RNA
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases require a free 3'-OH group to attack the incoming dNTP \( \alpha \)-phosphate. Because ddNTPs lack the 3'-OH group (having 3'-H instead), incorporation irreversibly terminates chain elongation.
